chapters.title: What we are building
chapters.summary: The goal in one sentence, the vocabulary the rest of the book depends on, and the test that will decide whether Odysseus works.

chapters.title: Three products, one design
chapters.summary: What Instinct, Muse and Grok Bot do, how each is built as far as anyone outside can tell, and where each has failed in public.

chapters.title: Anatomy of a personal agent
chapters.summary: The nine parts every such assistant needs, how a single request travels through them, and the one rule that keeps it safe: the model proposes, code grants.

chapters.title: Choosing the stack
chapters.summary: How each part was chosen, why the first proposal was thrown out, and how to read a benchmark that was run by the company it flatters.

chapters.title: The build plan
chapters.summary: Six stages, what each one proves, and the test each must pass before the next begins.

chapters.title: A thread that answers
chapters.summary: The thin Telegram slice, file by file: one allowed user, streamed replies, web search, a stop that works, a budget and a log. Tested against a stand-in, then run live, which found a bug and a slow start.

chapters.title: Memory that survives
chapters.summary: A small profile read in full, dated notes that are searched, a history of every change, and why every save is reported to the owner. Passed its test in one live run.

chapters.title: Speaking first
chapters.summary: Reminders sent by code, routines run by a read-only agent, three recorded outcomes for every run, and why the half-hourly check was left switched off. Passed its test in one live run with the clock moved by hand.

chapters.title: The gate
chapters.summary: Allow, ask or refuse; a question written by code and answered with a button; two independent locks. Then four holes found by reading the code, and what was done about each.

chapters.title: Hands: mail and calendar
chapters.summary: Reading and acting in the owner's mail and calendar through a connector service: ten narrow tools, each with its own rule. Read live; sending, changing and deleting have run only in a test world.

chapters.title: Hands: the browser
chapters.summary: Tasks handed to a vendor's browsing agent, for everything without a connector. The gate can only decide whether a run starts. For two days, by the owner's choice, it did not ask even then; after a second audit it asks again. The chapter says plainly what not asking gives up. Browsed two public pages live; one report was doubtful.

chapters.title: Eyes: reading files
chapters.summary: Documents the owner sends are turned into text by a recognition service and fenced off from the owner's own words. Pictures are shown to the model itself, which sees as well as reads. One test bill read; one generated picture seen.

chapters.title: A home that stays awake
chapters.summary: Moving from the owner's laptop to a small always-on server: an image, a machine, a disk and secrets, with no door open to the internet. Ran there for five minutes before the hosting service stopped it, which the chapter examines.

chapters.title: Measuring it
chapters.summary: An errand suite: the real agent against a seeded test world, scored by code on what is true afterwards. It found real faults, scored 97%, and was judged not good enough. The chapter explains why.

chapters.title: A world that does not hold still
chapters.summary: What the research on evaluation found, and the first version built from it: a world with time, events, other people and failing tools; properties checked on every run; every errand run reworded and under failure. Errands that passed every time as written failed one time in eleven.

chapters.title: A second channel: WhatsApp
chapters.summary: WhatsApp calls the program where Telegram is asked, so this channel needs a door, and three checks to guard it. Sending works for real; receiving waits on a server the internet can reach.

chapters.title: Not losing its place
chapters.summary: Three ways the first design lost the owner's work, and what replaced them: messages that wait their turn, a conversation that survives a restart, and a plain notice when a restart interrupts a task.

chapters.title: Ears: voice notes
chapters.summary: A voice note is turned into text, shown back to the owner, and then handled like any typed message. Checked end to end with a synthesized recording; no real voice yet.

chapters.title: Being told: watches
chapters.summary: "Tell me when Priya replies." The connector reports each new email or calendar change, a read-only small model judges it against what the owner asked for, and code does the telling. Run in the simulated world; not yet fired by a real email.

chapters.title: A second reading: what the tests did not find
chapters.summary: Every test passed and an independent reading still found sixteen things wrong: holes in the gate, failures nobody was told about, and numbers that left something out. What each was, what closed it, what the owner then relaxed, and what is still open.

chapters.title: The firm's database: Attio
chapters.summary: The first customer is named: a venture capital firm, one assistant per partner. Attio is reached through Attio's own server, signed in to by the owner with no key copied, its 58 tools offered through two and sorted by label and name. Read from live; a first layout of 21 fields and one list created on the owner's approval, by the coding agent and not yet by the assistant itself.
